raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old female presented to the emergency department with widespread pruritic, painful skin lesions, dyspnea, confusion, and a syncopal episode. Past medical history included BP with multiple BP flares, chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage IV, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
The patient takes several chronic medications. These include acetaminophen 500 mg as needed; amlodipine 5 mg daily; calcitriol 0.25 mcg twice a week; hydroxyzine 10 mg every 8 h as needed for anxiety and itchiness; insulin glargine 25 units at bedtime; melatonin 3 mg at bedtime as needed; and mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily.
In addition, the patient visited her dermatologist five days prior to presenting to the ED and was prescribed several new medications. These included prednisone 20 mg daily, to be gradually tapered; clobetasol topical ointment 0.05% twice daily on her right thigh; and miconazole topical cream 2% twice daily on her right thigh.
Her usual BP lesions included tense and flaccid bullae ranging from 5 to 10 mm in size, mostly populated over her abdomen, anterior thighs, and posterior upper arms. Her BP flares usually affected her right upper thigh, groin, and lower back and manifested as multiple vesicular and vesiculopustular lesions with an erythematous base. She had a BP flare 2 weeks prior to this presentation and was prescribed a prolonged oral prednisone taper (40 mg daily for 4 weeks, and then decreased dose by 10 mg every fourth week) by her dermatologist. But unlike her previous flares, the lesions did not respond to prednisone therapy, and she presented on current admission with several erosive vesicles on an erythematous base, predominantly concentrated over the sacral region and right thigh and some also scattered over her abdomen and face.
Vital signs included blood pressure 125/64 mmHg, pulse 102 bpm, respiratory rate 16/minute saturating 98% on room air, and temperature 97.2 F. Pertinent exam findings included sparse scattered non-erythematous erosive lesions on her face, white densely populated similar appearing lesions over her lower back, right lower abdomen, and right thigh circumferentially. Some of these lesions were escharesque and crusted, while others were oozing yellow exudate. Her mentation and other organ systems were unremarkable on examination.
Pertinent labs included white cell count 11,900/microL with 87% neutrophils, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (which was her baseline). Two sets of blood cultures stayed negative. Superficial skin cultures from the thigh wound grew Corynebacterium species and Streptococcus dysgalactiae. She was given a one-time intravenous vancomycin (1000 mg) initially which was adjusted with fluctuating renal function and started on piperacillin-tazobactam (2250 mg every 6 h). Prednisone was decreased to 20 mg daily.
On day 2 of hospitalization, she exhibited progressive fatigue, intermittent confusion and new-onset auditory hallucinations. CT head with contrast did not show any anomalies. MRI brain could not be done due to behavioral limitation with delirium. She was then evaluated by in-house dermatologist who recommended empiric initiation of oral valacyclovir (500 mg twice daily) with a suspicion for herpes zoster. On day 4, the mentation and renal function worsened. She had to be intubated for airway protection, and temporary dialysis was initiated. At this point, her prednisone and mycophenolate mofetil were held. Infectious disease consultation was sought. Viral culture by unroofing a new vesicle on the right lower abdomen was taken and she was switched to intravenous acyclovir (250 mg every 8 h). Piperacillin-tazobactam was de-escalated to ampicillin-sulbactam (3000 mg daily), while continuing vancomycin. Lumbar puncture could not be done because of skin lesions over the site of the procedure.
Viral culture of the skin lesion came back positive for VZV, as well as a separate PCR test positive on the same lesion. The remaining infectious work-up included a negative repeat blood culture, serum cryptococcal antigen, negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, negative urine histoplasma antigen, and negative HIV screen. Electroencephalogram study on day 4 revealed no epileptiform discharges.
From day 5 through day 11, despite gradual weaning off of sedation and pressor support, she continued to stay nonresponsive except for grimacing to painful stimulus. Further complications included worsening pancytopenia. Antibiotics were discontinued on day 10, while acyclovir was continued with the aim of at least 14 days. Goals of care discussion with family led to proceeding with comfort care, and the patient passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old female presented with widespread pruritic, painful skin lesions, dyspnea, confusion, and a syncopal episode.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a history of bullous pemphigoid (BP) flares typically manifesting as vesicles and bullae over the abdomen, thighs, and arms. Two weeks prior to admission, she experienced a presumed BP flare and was started on a prolonged oral prednisone taper (40 mg daily), and 5 days prior to presentation her dermatologist adjusted her regimen to prednisone 20 mg daily with topical clobetasol 0.05% and topical miconazole 2%. Unlike previous flares, the lesions failed to respond and progressed to erosive vesicles on an erythematous base over the sacrum, right thigh, abdomen, and face, accompanied by dyspnea, confusion, and syncope.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bullous pemphigoid with recurrent flares, chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage IV (baseline creatinine 3.2 mg/dL), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful pruritic skin lesions, dyspnea, confusion, and syncope. Home medications: mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg BID, prednisone 20 mg daily, clobetasol 0.05% ointment BID, miconazole 2% cream BID, acetaminophen 500 mg PRN, amlodipine 5 mg daily, calcitriol 0.25 mcg twice weekly, hydroxyzine 10 mg q8h PRN, insulin glargine 25 units QHS, and melatonin 3 mg QHS PRN.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: BP 125/64 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 97.2 F. Skin: sparse scattered non-erythematous erosive lesions on the face, and densely populated white erosive, crusted, eschar-like, and yellow-exudative vesicular lesions over the lower back, sacral region, right lower abdomen, and circumferential right thigh. Mentation and other organ systems were initially unremarkable on exam; on hospital day 2 she developed delirium and auditory hallucinations, and by day 4 she required intubation for airway protection.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs: WBC 11,900/uL (87% neutrophils), Hb 11.2 g/dL, sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline). Microbiology: two sets of blood cultures negative; superficial thigh wound cultures grew Corynebacterium species and Streptococcus dysgalactiae.
objective.advanced_workup: CT head with contrast (day 2): no acute anomalies (MRI brain deferred due to delirium; LP deferred due to overlying sacral skin lesions). EEG (day 4): no epileptiform discharges. Infectious workup: unroofed right lower abdominal vesicle viral culture and PCR both positive for Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV); repeat blood cultures, serum cryptococcal antigen, SARS-CoV-2 PCR, urine Histoplasma antigen, and HIV screen all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infection with secondary cutaneous bacterial superinfection and encephalopathy in an immunocompromised patient on mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone (histoplasmosis ruled out by negative urine Histoplasma antigen). Confirmation: Positive VZV viral culture and positive VZV PCR from an unroofed abdominal skin vesicle. Plan & clinical course: Initially treated with IV vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam (de-escalated to ampicillin-sulbactam), and oral valacyclovir, then switched on day 4 to IV acyclovir (250 mg q8h) while holding mycophenolate and prednisone and initiating hemodialysis and mechanical ventilation. Complicated by persistent coma, worsening pancytopenia, and renal failure; transitioned to comfort care per family goals of care and passed away.
